articles.title: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
articles.author: Doug Bock Clark
paras: In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.
The board sets the swing state’s election rules, oversees the conduct of its election officials and investigates allegations of fraud.

Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allied organizations on shared priorities. Among them: advancing the use of a controversial, error-prone software tool known as ELLY to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.

The state board’s current vice chair, Janelle King, and her predecessor, Janice Johnston, have both attended meetings of EIN or VoterGA, an aligned organization whose membership and goals significantly overlap with EIN. Johnston retired in June but still plays an active role in state election matters behind the scenes.
At an August 2025 fundraiser for VoterGA, Mitchell declared she loved Johnston and King, who were both present. “You know, we’ve worked so hard together,” Mitchell said.

At least three members of the state board’s eight-person professional staff have participated in EIN meetings, including people who handle allegations of voter fraud and misconduct by election officials.

The board’s executive director, James Mills, likewise has worked closely with members of the EIN, according to five sources with knowledge of these interactions, board documents and EIN communications shared with ProPublica.

EIN’s close ties to the board and its staff have given it extraordinary influence over how elections are run in Georgia, experts said. In particular, the group has been able to enlist the board’s help in getting counties to remove voters from their rolls based on information from ELLY.

“Trump allies captured the State Election Board to keep claims of a stolen 2020 election going and tilt Georgia elections toward Republicans,” said Max Flugrath, a director at Fair Fight Action, a voting advocacy nonprofit that has closely tracked the board’s and the network’s actions. “EIN was the behind-the-scenes driver spearheading these changes.”
The board’s chair, John Fervier, told ProPublica he had not known about EIN’s sway over the board or its staff, but said he’d long sensed that an outside force was shaping the board’s actions.

“The more I look into this, the more I’m realizing that the Election Integrity Network has been having an undue influence on the State Election Board, and that needs to cease,” he said in an interview, though he declined to go into specifics about personnel matters. “I’m looking forward to changes in how the election board operates.”
Fervier has called a special meeting for Friday, in part to discuss personnel matters.

In response, Garland Favorito, an EIN leader and head of VoterGA, called on social media for his followers to inundate state board members with messages defending Mills and other staffers associated with the group.

“There is a significant possibility that these members will vote to terminate the Executive Director, investigators or possibly even staff members, any of which would destroy the SEB as we now know it,” Favorito wrote on Wednesday, referring to the State Election Board. “As most of you know, the SEB staff has made remarkable historical progress this year in … accountability for election corruption and much more. The Executive Director and staff deserve raises for amazing performances, not threats of termination.”

In interviews in late September, Johnston did not directly answer questions about her relationship to EIN. “I’m all about election integrity, wherever it comes from,” she said. She acknowledged she had remained involved with board affairs after her retirement. “It gets in your blood,” she said. Two days later, she posted on social media that “Cleta Mitchell, Election Integrity expert has the right ideas” about how elections should be run.
Johnston did not answer detailed questions about her relationship with EIN and affiliated groups.

King acknowledged she spoke about election matters with activists from EIN and VoterGA, but said they did not influence her decisions. She also said she saw no problem with EIN activists working for the board, though the staff is supposed to be independent and nonpartisan.
“As long as they are representing the SEB well, fine,” she said in an interview. “If they choose to become members of an organization in their private time, that is their choice.”

When a reporter recounted instances in which staffers had worked to advance EIN goals in their official capacity, she said she was unaware of this. “That is the first I’ve heard about it,” she responded.
Mills declined to answer questions from ProPublica about his relationship to EIN.

Mitchell did not respond directly to ProPublica but, after receiving detailed questions, put a post on X celebrating EIN’s work with the election board. “An election integrity group is working with election officials to oversee elections,” she wrote. “Wow! What a discovery!!! Pulitzer anyone?”
Favorito called the idea that the board and its staff had been working secretly with the EIN and VoterGA a “patently false conspiracy theory.”
EIN has been deeply entwined with conservatives’ efforts to reshape Georgia elections since at least 2024.

That year, ProPublica’s reporting revealed, EIN members secretly pushed a rule through the State Election Board allowing local officials to potentially delay certifying the state’s vote count. A court subsequently struck down the change, which experts had warned could enable county election boards to disrupt certifying the election if Trump had lost.

In late 2025, the board played a role in instigating the Trump administration’s unprecedented effort to reinvestigate alleged 2020 voting irregularities, formally asking the Justice Department to obtain Fulton County election records subsequently seized by the FBI. It was a move pushed by the EIN. The affidavit authorizing the raid cited Johnston and King as witnesses. The affidavit also cited a report put together by an EIN researcher compiling activists’ debunked allegations of fraud.

In recent months, EIN’s allies and participants at the state board pushed counties to use ELLY, a tool developed by an EIN member, to search voter rolls for signs of fraud and purge suspect registrants.

ELLY aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources, but doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as Social Security numbers or full dates of birth. As a result, voting rights groups have said, ELLY often erroneously flags legitimate voters.

Nonetheless, before the midterms, the State Election Board’s investigative staff pressured Chatham County, a Democratic stronghold, to purge more than 200 registered voters that the tool identified as questionable, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported.

After the election, a Forsyth County election board member who is also a member of EIN submitted ELLY data questioning the validity of over 60 ballots, including four cast by people who were supposedly dead. ProPublica found that all four were, in fact, alive. The board rejected the challenges.
EIN members and state board officials have defended ELLY’s accuracy.

The EIN’s connections to the board carry additional importance in light of last week’s election results, in which Democrats wrested control of all statewide offices and the state House from Republicans. The House appoints a member to the State Election Board, opening the door to change.
Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms ran on a platform that promised a new approach to the election board.

“The State Election Board has become mired in political games, conspiracy theories, and partisan interference,” the platform stated. Bottoms’ platform pledged that she would “work with the General Assembly to eliminate the current State Election Board and replace it with a stronger, more independent election oversight structure that is insulated from partisan manipulation.”
Fervier is part of the board’s four-member Republican majority, but he has clashed repeatedly with Johnston, King and Mills and has effectively been relegated to a member of the minority at times.

Emails and communications between board members and staff obtained by ProPublica via public records requests show that Fervier and other board members who oppose steps supported by the EIN have been excluded from some board hiring decisions.

Earlier this year, Fervier publicly accused Mills of going beyond what the board had authorized in calling for the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security to intervene to assess the security of the state’s voting machines.

“Activists should not control the board,” he told ProPublica. “I’m really looking forward to this meeting because I think that we’re going to address some issues that should have been addressed awhile ago.”

articles.title: His Church or His Child? A Sixth-Generation Member of a Faith-Healing Sect Had to Choose.
articles.author: Teresa Mahoney
paras: What if you had to pick between your deeply held faith and the life of your child? That’s the gutting choice that faced Marshall Phillips, an Oregon dad who was born into the Followers of Christ, a sect whose creed bars medical treatment. When his 11-year-old son was stricken with a dire health crisis, Phillips became caught between his faith, his family and the state of Oregon, which had begun cracking down on faith-healing parents who don’t seek medical help for their minor children. A decade later, Phillips was pulled into another one of his church’s life-or-death dramas when he was asked to care for a newborn whose twin had died because her parents had refused to seek medical attention.

To examine the power of faith-healing churches and the toll of their teachings, The Oregonian investigative reporter Noelle Crombie, senior staff photojournalist Beth Nakamura and videographer Samantha Swindler spent months with Phillips and his family, piecing together rare accounts from inside the deeply shuttered world of the Followers of Christ and of the state officials who fought to protect children who need medical treatment. The documentary, produced by The Oregonian’s managing producer of video, Teresa Mahoney, not only lays out in visceral detail the agonizing choices that families like the Phillips have to make, it also chronicles how they overcame the clash with their religious beliefs.
Go inside the secretive Followers of Christ sect and watch the extraordinary journey.Read more in this riveting print narrative, and meet the man who dominated and shaped the sect.

articles.title: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
articles.author: Ben Berke
paras: On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts.
Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components for wind power out to sea.

He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast.
Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which Biden spoke.

A 20-minute drive east, in New Bedford, hundreds of workers who helped assemble wind turbine parts from Canada and Europe over the last three years have given way to seagulls and geese. The birds shuffle along the now-empty pier the state of Massachusetts spent $140 million to build for offshore wind development.
In nearby Providence, Rhode Island, a newly built factory that manufactured offshore wind turbine foundation platforms has emptied out.

Amid the Trump administration’s multifront war against offshore wind, the cost on the ground in New England, the launchpad of the country’s offshore wind industry, can be seen in empty warehouses, silent marine terminals and ledgers recording hundreds of millions of dollars of state investment that may not be recouped.
ProPublica partnered with Ocean State Media, The Connecticut Mirror and the New Bedford Light to document the consequences of the administration’s efforts.

Many offshore wind projects faced a precarious future before President Donald Trump retook office. Rising construction costs driven by inflation and supply chain shortages forced some developers to back out of contracts to build wind farms and supply electricity to states. Various groups have also fought construction of projects saying they disrupt marine ecosystems and mar coastal views.

But last year, the administration temporarily forced five projects to stop construction, further clouding the horizon. Courts allowed the developers to proceed, but that has not eliminated the threat. Last month, the U.S. Department of the Interior asked a court for permission to reconsider a key permit for one of those five projects, Revolution Wind, which is already up and running and can power more than 350,000 New England homes at maximum capacity.

The administration also has frozen future development on all offshore wind farms, including a cluster of projects that haven’t been built but proposed to power up to 1.7 million New England homes. It has blocked or is seeking review of the permits that would allow these to be built. Meanwhile, the administration is paying other wind developers billions of dollars to sell back their leases and walk away.

At a press conference Monday, Trump said he supports a bipartisan bill that would accelerate U.S. energy development. When a reporter pointed out that the bill includes wind energy, Trump said he would not approve “wind turbines ’cause wind turbines are a major loser.”
The upheaval has had ripple effects. The cable company Biden touted decided not to build its factory, citing “long-term trends in the U.S. market.”
Port cities like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, Connecticut, are left trying to hold onto the economic gains they have made building wind farms.
The Connecticut Mirror: Offshore wind offered a ‘limitless’ future for Connecticut. Trump scuttled the plan.
The New Bedford Light: Fishermen’s offshore wind work drying up
Ocean State Media: Offshore wind saved a struggling New Bedford union. Now its future is uncertain.

As recently as last winter, New Bedford, a historic whaling and textile manufacturing center, had hotels, offices and piers buzzing with offshore wind workers. Local businesses from caterers to cleaners to fuel suppliers landed new contracts servicing the wind industry.

In New London — another port once central to the whaling industry — officials worked with one of the world’s largest wind developers to pump more than $300 million of public and private funds into a state-owned pier. Despite significant cost overruns and some early construction challenges, the effort transformed the pier into a staging area for the wind industry.

Over the last four years, the pier has been a hive of activity. Hundreds of workers were employed loading and offloading turbine parts — with blades the length of a football field — from specially designed ships, some with names drawn from Greek mythology. Local companies also found work supporting the industry, including one that offered water rescue training for people working on construction sites offshore.
“I think the future just looked limitless,” said New London Mayor Michael Passero.

Before wind, Passero said that officials tried for years to attract different industries to the pier, which is overshadowed by larger port facilities in New York and Boston. It was often used to import and store large piles of road salt.
The most recent wind project based at the pier is scheduled to finish work next year. Port officials have yet to find a tenant to occupy the space.
“They’ll be back to the old days of trying to lure cargo here,” Passero said.

Amid Trump’s war on wind, a frontline of union and nonunion workers watches opportunity disappear. One project alone, Vineyard Wind, directly employed a total of more than 3,700 full- and part-time workers — most of them from Massachusetts — over eight years of development and construction, according to the developer.

During peak construction activity, as many as 300 union members worked onshore in southeastern Massachusetts for the project, the first large offshore wind farm fully permitted by the federal government. The wind farm was completed this year.

Longshoreman Onix Vazquez, 34, worked full-time tying up barges and moving turbine components on and off New Bedford’s wind pier. He grew up a few blocks away and said he had struggled to find lucrative work until Vineyard Wind began hiring from his union.

Vazquez’s hourly wage of $50 was nearly double what he previously earned unloading occasional shipments of tangerines and juice concentrate. It allowed him and other members of his historically Black union to make down payments on houses, pay off medical bills and for the first time take their families on out-of-state vacations.
“Most of us have to get other jobs for now or collect unemployment,” said Kevin Rose, president of New Bedford’s longshoremen union, which put about two dozen members to work on the project.

The union had been planning to rebuild its nearby meeting hall, which was demolished a decade earlier when work grew scarce. But the next developer to lease New Bedford’s wind pier has delayed its project indefinitely. The union members have put the plans for their new hall on hold.
Vazquez said he now works a seasonal job in the cranberry industry for much lower pay.
“They don’t see that it affects us, the ones that work the projects,” he said.

In response to questions about the impact of the administration’s actions on American offshore wind workers, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of the Interior repeated criticisms of offshore wind as an expensive and unreliable source of energy.

“The reality is that the Biden administration lured companies into these projects with the promise of millions of taxpayer dollars in subsidies to make these offshore wind projects viable,” the spokesperson said in an email.
The view is more nuanced on the ground. New Bedford’s fishing industry is generally critical of wind farm development because fishermen worry about disruption to fishing grounds.
But fishing catch limits keep boats tied to docks for much of the year. Work for wind farms gets them out to sea and helps pay the bills.

Over the past few years of construction, Vineyard Wind paid about $11 million to 55 fishing vessels from New England and an estimated 60 to 70 fishermen, according to the developer. (The figure also covers fuel.) The fishermen look out for protected species, guard exposed underwater cable as it’s being laid and log information for the developer.
Some fishermen say they will work in offshore wind for as long as they can.

“The scallop boats need the extra revenue,” said Patrick Walsh, 37, a fifth-generation fisherman who plans to rejoin his father’s fishing business when wind work wraps up. “The worst thing for a boat is to sit. Those boats are made to work.”
Wind farm work made it possible for him to buy his first house, he said.
“Fishing would pay bills, and wind was going in the bank.”
The post How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
articles.author: Sarahbeth Maney
paras: The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans.
In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.”

It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.” And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.”
But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President Donald Trump returned to office.
They are not just numbers.

Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday.
Over the past year, several of these people shared the lingering effects of what happened to them with ProPublica.
Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan
“We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held.” Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan

In September 2025, Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan learned that ICE agents had intercepted members of her family as they drove one of her uncles to a court hearing. Ramirez Sanan, then 17, said she rushed to the scene and discovered agents had broken the car windows and pulled her two uncles, her mother and her younger brother out. Video of the incident showed agents kicking and slamming Ramirez Sanan’s mother to the ground and then twisting her arms to handcuff her. Ramirez Sanan said she saw other agents questioning her brother against a fence, threatening to arrest him if he couldn’t prove he had legal status.
Both she and her brother are citizens.

“Him being a 13-year-old with autism, he doesn’t understand these things like we do. He didn’t know what ‘a legal status’ is. He’s not able to tell them: ‘Yes, I have a legal status. I’m born here,’” Ramirez Sanan said. She said that when she rushed toward her mom and brother, begging agents to let them go, they detained her. “It was really scary thinking that they might have taken us and deported us to Guatemala, where we don’t have anything.”

DHS said that its agents intercepted the car in order to detain the uncle who was going to court that day, and that they “used the appropriate force necessary.” He was facing charges of sexual assault on a child and remains in ICE custody. He has pleaded not guilty.

As for Ramirez Sanan, her mother and her brother, they were released the day of the incident. Her mother, who has lived in the United States for 20 years and has a green card, was treated at a hospital for a concussion, bruising and nerve damage in one of her arms.
DHS denies that they were ever detained.

“We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held,” said Ramirez Sanan, who struggled with anxiety and depression after the incident. “I lost my whole senior year fighting this. My brother isn’t the same either.”

In June 2025, Andrea Velez was dropped off at work at a shoe company in downtown Los Angeles and inadvertently walked into an immigration raid on street vendors. She said one of the masked agents rushed toward her, grabbed her and slammed her to the pavement. Velez said she attempted to shield herself with her work bag.

“Throughout the whole time, I kept saying I was a U.S. citizen,” Velez recalled, saying that agents called her an “alleged U.S. citizen” even after they checked her ID. “They kept saying how many ‘bodies they got’ that day.”

Velez said that she was detained for two days, and that she was denied an opportunity to call family or a lawyer for most of that time. The government charged Velez with assault. DHS said she “made physical contact” with agents and tried to impede them. A judge ultimately dismissed the case.
After her arrest, Velez said she was so afraid of being detained again that she worked remotely and avoided going outside.

In January, not long after immigration agents in Minneapolis had shot and killed an American woman named Renee Good, Quentin Williams, a teaching assistant at nearby Roosevelt High School, was guiding students toward buses when more agents arrived outside his building.
Williams said that agents began confronting students and staff. At some point during the commotion, he said, the agents threw him to the ground and choked him so hard he couldn’t breathe.
“They didn’t even know what they were doing — just kind of being reckless [with] assault rifles out and pepper-spraying staff after they took me down,” Williams recalled.
Agents drove Williams to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building, where they detained him for several hours.

Later, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi published his photo on her social media accounts, describing him as a “Minnesota rioter.” Federal authorities issued a warrant for his arrest for assaulting officers. The charges against him were eventually dismissed, and he’s filed a claim against the government for damages over his arrest.

Williams said he’s still haunted by the idea that he came close to meeting the same fates as Good and George Floyd, who was killed by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. “I didn’t leave the house for at least up to a week,” he said. “I felt lucky to be alive.”
Anabel Romero, John Carter, Juana Rodriguez and their children

In October 2025, some 200 federal agents and local police officers in armored vehicles, a helicopter and on horseback conducted a raid on a racetrack in Wilder, Idaho, and detained hundreds of people, including dozens of children. Among them ProPublica identified at least 30 U.S. citizens.
Anabel Romero had left her kids eating in the car while she went to look at the horses. They were on opposite sides of the track when the raid began.

Romero said the agents wore camouflage and had their guns drawn. She had no idea who they were. So she ran and tried to hide. “They didn’t identify themselves,” Romero said. “I didn’t know who they were.”
She said unidentified officers tackled her, zip-tied her and threatened to “fucking blow your head off.”

On the other side of the track, Romero’s 14-year-old daughter, SueHey Tello, said officers surrounded their car, pointing guns at her brother, 6, and sister, 8. When Tello refused to exit the car without her younger siblings, agents pulled her so roughly out of the car that she fell, leaving bruises. She said agents zip-tied her hands.

Romero and Tello said the agents refused to remove the zip ties for hours, despite Tello’s age. The teenager said the incident has affected her view of law enforcement. Her mother says that the 6-year-old still has nightmares. Officers are meant “to keep us safe,” Tello said. “But yet they treated all of us like that.”

John Carter was working security at the track when the raid started. He had brought his girlfriend and his two children along with him. He recalls officers throwing a flash-bang near him and his son, and then the officers detained them. “They cinched the zip ties down as tight as they could,” Carter said. He said the officers also zip-tied his 14-year-old daughter but removed the restraints when he complained.
Carter explained that he is active in the local Republican Party and a strong supporter of law enforcement. But he said that what he saw officers doing that day was wrong.
“Things are supposed to be done humanely and correctly,” he said. “This wasn’t.”

The agents also detained Juana Rodriguez, who attended the event with her family. She said that she was zip-tied beside her 3-year-old son, which left her unable to pick him up and comfort him during the long hours they waited to prove their citizenship. “He wanted me to hug him, to hold him,” Rodriguez said. She and her son are both U.S. citizens and lead plaintiffs in an ACLU of Idaho lawsuit alleging the raid illegally targeted Latinos. ICE, the FBI and several Idaho agencies have denied the charge and asked that the lawsuit be dismissed.

DHS did not respond to any specific allegations made by Rodriguez, Romero, Carter or their families. Instead, a spokesperson wrote in an email statement that the raid successfully helped dismantle an illegal gambling operation, and that ICE officers “didn’t zip tie, restrain or arrest any children.” The FBI declined to comment to ProPublica but told local media no “young children” were zip-tied. DHS, the FBI and multiple Idaho law enforcement agencies have refused to share the number of U.S. citizens held that day.
“I didn’t want to walk to my apartment by myself; I didn’t want to be out in the dark by myself.” Amanda Trebach

In August 2025, Amanda Trebach, a nurse and volunteer with an immigrant advocacy organization, said she was monitoring ICE activities outside a facility that the agency was using to stage operations when agents grabbed her and pinned her to the ground, kneeling on her neck and back. They shoved her into the back of a van and held her for several hours until taking her to a federal detention facility in Los Angeles. She was not given the opportunity to speak with an attorney during the 33 hours that she was in custody. She said agents took her phone and never returned it.

DHS said Trebach was detained because she attempted to physically impede its agents’ operations by jumping in front of moving vehicles, hitting their cars with her protest signs and shouting obscenities at agents. She denies this.
She said that after the incident she felt paranoid that she was being followed.
“I didn’t want to walk to my apartment by myself; I didn’t want to be out in the dark by myself,” she said. “I didn’t know if they were going to come get me.”

George Retes, a U.S. Army veteran who served in Iraq, was driving into work at a cannabis farm in July 2025 and arrived to find the place being raided by immigration agents. Protesters had gathered outside the farm. He found himself trapped between the agents and the protesters. The agents broke his car window, pepper-sprayed him and pulled him out onto the ground. He was detained for three days, missing his daughter’s third birthday. Retes said, agents refused to explain why he’d been detained or to let him call relatives or a lawyer.
When ProPublica published Retes’ story last year, he said agents knew he was a citizen.
“They didn’t care,” he recalled. “They still sent me away to jail.”
DHS officials made statements claiming Retes had assaulted their agents. But he was never charged.

In June 2025, immigration agents conducted a raid on an auto shop owned by Javier Ramirez and his family. He said agents swept him up as they were detaining his workers. He recalled hearing one of the agents yell: “Hey, just get him! He’s Mexican.” He said agents tackled him and one of them put a knee on his face. He recalled hearing the agents boasting about the numbers of immigrants they were detaining across the city that day, saying: “How many did you get? I got 10, I got 15.” According to a lawsuit that Ramirez filed against DHS, he said he was held in federal custody for four days and was denied medication he needs for diabetes. DHS has not filed a response to the lawsuit, but previously the agency said that Ramirez was arrested for obstructing law enforcement, and that it never denied him medication.

When Jeane “Bleu” Wong, an operator of a daycare center and activist, heard in July 2025 that ICE agents had arrived at a nearby apartment complex, she rushed to the scene to provide assistance to people who were being detained. Agents detained her when she tried to remove one of their masks.

She was held in the San Ysidro Port of Entry, the largest and busiest land border crossing in the Western Hemisphere, and later moved to a federal prison. Wong said that during her time in custody she was strip-searched and shackled in chains that restricted her from using the restroom. Federal authorities charged Wong with assaulting a federal agent. She eventually pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor.

A little over a year later, Wong received a notice from the California Department of Social Services that her license to care for children had been revoked because of the assault. She and her wife are selling their home and relocating outside of Southern California.
“We could totally fight, and I’d probably win,” she said. “But we don’t have the money, time, energy.”
“I was begging them, ‘Just let me breathe!’” Rafie Ollah Shouhed

Rafie Ollah Shouhed, 79, was born in Iran, moved to Los Angeles after the Islamic Revolution and became a U.S. citizen. On Sept. 9, 2025, Shouhed, owner of Valley Car Wash, watched with alarm as immigration agents stormed into his business and attempted to detain his employees. He rushed outside to see what was going on. Security video of the incident shows agents knocked Shouhed to the ground repeatedly. He told agents that he had just had heart surgery. “They were sitting on me,” he recalled. “I was begging them, ‘Just let me breathe!’” He said in an ongoing lawsuit that the agents kept him handcuffed for 12 hours and left him with injuries to his arm, elbows and ribs. Shouhed said that he’s still receiving treatment for his injuries, and that he has quit working. DHS said Shouhed was arrested for interfering with and assaulting officers and did not answer questions about his lawsuit. He was released without charges.

Leonardo Garcia Venegas was laying concrete with his construction crew in Alabama in May 2025 when immigration agents arrived at the site without a warrant and began detaining his co-workers, including his brother. Garcia Venegas pulled out his phone to film the agents. Videos he and other workers recorded show agents approaching to arrest Garcia Venegas while he filmed, tackling and arresting him while he yelled that he was a U.S. citizen. Garcia Venegas said that he told the agents he had his REAL ID on him, but that they dismissed the document as fake. They held him in handcuffs for an hour before finally releasing him without charges. DHS said he was impeding officers. After that first incident, immigration agents detained Garcia Venegas two more times, each time ignoring statements and identification documents that prove he is a U.S. citizen.

Garcia Venegas filed a lawsuit against DHS over its warrantless raids on construction sites. DHS responded to the lawsuit, saying that its agents didn’t need warrants to operate at construction sites because they’re open to the public. The agency also said that brief stops like Garcia Venegas’ were “reasonable.” Until the case is resolved, a judge ordered a temporary halt to the operations.
“I just want to live in peace,” he told ProPublica after his third arrest.
“Nobody ever asked me for ID, my name or my citizenship.” Aliya Rahman

Aliya Rahman, who is autistic and disabled, was driving to a doctor’s appointment in January when she reached an intersection where protesters were confronting immigration officers. She said several agents swarmed her car and yelled at her to move out of the way. They broke her window and pulled her from the car.
“Nobody ever asked me for ID, my name or my citizenship,” Rahman said.
DHS said agents detained Rahman because she ignored their instructions. She denied that, saying that she was confused and saw no way to move without hitting someone.
She said agents then shackled her feet and held her in a detention cell at the federal building. She passed out and awoke in a hospital room. She was released without charges later that day.

In January, Jeyli Salguero awoke when she heard someone banging on her door and then the sound of the door breaking open. Federal agents, their guns drawn, rushed inside and told her family they were looking for her brother.

“We told them yes he lived here, but he doesn’t live here anymore,” Salguero said she told the agents. “They started getting a bit more angry and were like, ‘Since you’re not collaborating, we’re gonna start checking your status.’” An agent grabbed Salguero’s phone and ordered Salguero to face a wall. In an ongoing lawsuit, Salguero has said that the agents entered the home without a valid warrant. DHS said that agents were searching for a fugitive, and that it has suspended the policy of entering homes without a judicial warrant.

Her father has temporary protected status but had not received paperwork showing that his status had been renewed. He was handcuffed and then detained for a month. Salguero’s older sister, who was undocumented, was handcuffed and deported to El Salvador. The rest of her family is now planning to sell their home and move to El Salvador. “It’s been a mental toll — a very big mental toll on all of us.”

Juan Muñoz, an elected member of the Board of Trustees that governs Oak Park Township outside of Chicago, was participating in an October protest outside the Broadview ICE Detention Center when he said that he was knocked to the ground by the commander of the Border Patrol. “When I looked up,” Muñoz recalled, “it was Commander Greg Bovino who was standing over me.” In depositions, Bovino denied tackling Muñoz, saying videos of the arrests showed no “reportable uses of force.”
Muñoz said agents knocked away his phone and zip-tied his hands. “Every agent that I encountered, I told the same thing, ‘I’m an elected official.’ No response.”

Muñoz was held inside of the detention center for eight hours before agents dropped him off at a gas station, without explaining why he’d been held. “They were over capacity, keeping people for way longer than that facility was intended for,” he recalled about the detention center. “It was filthy. They don’t have proper hygiene products or are able to feed people properly,” Muñoz said. DHS did not comment on his specific detention. But, referring to Muñoz and other protesters detained with him, it posted a comment on social media, saying, “We will NOT allow violent activists to lay hands on our law enforcement.”

In October 2025, Chicago Alderperson Jessie Fuentes said she rushed to a local emergency room because she’d been told that ICE agents had been spotted inside. She identified herself to the agents as an elected official and began asking them whether they’d obtained a warrant. Video taken of the incident shows that agents grabbed and handcuffed her. Fuentes was held for 15 minutes, during which time members of her staff posted the video online and her supporters gathered outside the hospital to demand her release. DHS, in a written statement, told ProPublica that Fuentes was put in “handcuffs but NEVER placed under arrest.”
“These individuals are operating above the law,” Fuentes said. “They’re operating with impunity.”

Caitlin Arwen was scrolling through a Facebook group for moms in October when she noticed a shared post that said immigration agents were detaining people in her town, which is about an hour’s drive outside of Chicago. Later that day she saw some of the vehicles that had been posted on Facebook and began following them, honking her horn to alert residents of their presence. One of the vehicles slammed on its brakes. U.S. marshals who were working with ICE surrounded her car, broke her window and pulled her out.

“They threw me on the broken glass, and they were all on top of me. I couldn’t breathe,” she recalled. Arwen estimates she was kept handcuffed face down on broken glass for roughly 35 minutes. “They taunted me, took photos of me, called me names, berated me and acted like I was somehow deserving of this.” DHS referred questions about Arwen’s arrest to the U.S. Marshals Service. A spokesperson for the service said Arwen’s arrest was a “task force arrest” and declined further comment.

Arwen was taken to a hospital, where marshals handcuffed her to the bed. After she was discharged, agents shackled her and moved her to a DHS detention facility, where she was not allowed to contact a lawyer or anyone else for help. “I didn’t have access to water or food the whole time,” said Arwen, adding that she was held for several hours. “Nobody showed me their badge all day. No one identified themselves. No one once read me my Miranda rights.”
Though federal officials declined to prosecute Arwen, state authorities charged her with traffic violations and obstruction of law enforcement. She has pleaded not guilty.
The post More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive.
articles.author: Doug Bock Clark
paras: Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting their ballots.

The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters.
But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots.

The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats swept statewide offices.

The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and rules. Mitchell worked closely with Donald Trump in his attempt to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election and, since he retook the presidency, has been central to his push to assert greater federal control over voting.

In the run-up to the midterms, on right-wing media and on private organizing calls, EIN participants outlined plans to search voter rolls with a software tool known as ELLY’s Election Monitor and contest ballots the tool deemed suspicious.

ELLY was developed by EIN member Rick Richards. It aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources. In Georgia, State Election Board members and top staffers have urged counties to use the tool to search their voter rolls for signs of fraud.

Richards talked about ELLY’s national potential on a podcast in late September, on which right-wing media personalities and activists touted its capacity to help GOP candidates contest their defeats. “We can prove the fraud that’s gone on in every state,” one commentator said. “This data will be able to set up challenges to those who lose.”

The following month, on a private call with EIN members and other conservative activists, Richards promised to provide data from more than 3,000 counties to “citizen monitors” and GOP candidates to try to prove fraud, according to a recording reviewed by ProPublica.

In an interview, Richards told ProPublica that he gave Clavijo data on Forsyth County at Clavijo’s request. He said in a subsequent email that their actions were meant to inform the board and remain confidential. Clavijo didn’t respond to questions from ProPublica.
Richards refused to answer questions about whether Clavijo’s effort was part of a wider EIN campaign to contest votes cast in the midterms.
“That’s irrelevant,” he said. “The data is the data. People can use it for what they want to.”
Mitchell, EIN’s leader, didn’t respond to questions about the group’s plans related to ELLY, either in Georgia or nationally.

In the months since some on Georgia’s State Election Board started promoting ELLY’s use, its accuracy has been much debated. The tool doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as voters’ Social Security or driver’s license numbers or full dates of birth, which increases the potential for mismatches involving people with the same names.
Voting rights groups have called ELLY error-prone. The Cherokee County election director complained to the state board after the tool falsely flagged a county board member’s spouse as dead.

State Election Board members and Richards have defended ELLY. Accusations that the data is unreliable were “horse hockey,” Richards told ProPublica, explaining this was “a Southern colloquialism for B.S.”

Late last week, according to several people familiar with the matter, Clavijo circulated documents to board members and Forsyth County’s election director. Based on data from ELLY, Clavijo questioned whether the names of more than 22,000 people on the county’s voter roll were correct and disputed the eligibility of 69 voters. In addition to four he claimed were deceased, he alleged others had moved out of the county or state, had voter ID irregularities or had registered under fictitious names, giving an initial as their first name.

During the meeting, Clavijo claimed that he was not trying to disrupt the election’s certification or formally challenge the voters, a process outlined in statutes that can lead to ballots being tossed or voters removed from the rolls. (Richards also said they had not formally challenged ballots.) Clavijo said he was merely seeking “to clean the voter rolls” and inform the board so officials could investigate further.

But other board members accused him of doing an end run around the formal challenge process. Barbara Luth, the board chair, said she felt “sorry for” Clavijo because activists were bypassing the challenge procedure “by coming to you and having you submit it.”
Under fire from fellow board members, Clavijo admitted he could not vouch for the data’s accuracy.
“I did not make any explicit accusation that the information was 100% correct,” he said.
The cover letter Clavijo submitted with the challenges said that they had not been verified with any “human review,” according to sources familiar with the matter.

Richards and Clavijo submitted obituaries for the voters they claimed were dead, but there were discrepancies between the information in them and the voters’ records. All of the obituaries said or suggested the deceased lived outside of Forsyth County, which would have made it impossible to vote there. One said the person lived in Arizona.
ProPublica confirmed that all four are actually alive.
Alexis Ramirez, a night-shift nurse, told ProPublica that she cast her ballot during early voting. She was surprised to hear her vote had been contested — and why.
“It’s kind of crazy that they attempted to do that without trying to prove it first,” she said.
Saramma George, another voter Richards and Clavijo claimed was dead, said she was “really angry” to have the validity of her ballot questioned.
In the third case, ProPublica spoke with a voter’s son, who said she was alive but didn’t want to talk to ProPublica. Her “ballot is valid,” he said.
The fourth voter, Chris Strickland, said, “I don’t know where they’re getting their information from, but it’s false. I’m alive. I’m here.”
The majority of the challenges — 38 of them, according to people familiar with the matter — involved voters who’d registered using an initial.

One voter, Alexander Knight, told ProPublica that he goes by his middle name and that the information in voter records mirrors how Department of Driver Services officials suggested he be identified on his driver’s license.
“I am real,” he told ProPublica.

Four other challenged voters said they, too, abbreviated their first names. A. Joseph Guntherberg confirmed he routinely used the same formulation of his name, adding that blocking his ballot would not help the challengers: “My candidate didn’t win.”
Richards said it was up to county election workers to check ELLY’s data — he merely gathers it to facilitate efforts to maintain accurate voter lists.

But at the meeting, Joel Natt, a Republican board member, said the responsibility lay with challengers to justify their accusations. “This has no relevance to anybody here until” they provide solid evidence, he said, “through the proper channel.”
The post A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive. appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin.
articles.author: Noelle Crombie
paras: The deputy medical examiner thought the family was being evasive. Eric Tonsfeldt had been dispatched to the pistachio-green house in Oregon City on the night of March 5, 2017. Inside he found Sarah Mitchell in bed, her dead newborn in her arms.

Mitchell is a member of the Followers of Christ, a sect known for refusing medical treatment. She had received no prenatal care. Three women without medical training guided her delivery that afternoon.

Tonsfeldt listened as the family insisted that the baby, whom they had named Ginnifer, had seemed healthy for most of the afternoon, then suddenly stopped breathing. They couldn’t explain why the baby appeared so underweight. Their answers to many of Tonsfeldt’s questions were vague. Nobody would make eye contact with him.

Later, investigators would discover that 13 minutes after Ginnifer’s birth, Followers began exchanging a series of worried texts. “Not good breathing,” one wrote in a group chat. Another requested prayers: “She’s really bad.” (One person in the chat would later advise deleting the messages.)

No one had called 911 as the gaps between each breath increased. When asked why not, Ginnifer’s father later said, “Because it’s in God’s hands.” He anointed his daughter with olive oil and wept as he prayed that she would be OK. Ginnifer died in his arms at 7 p.m., four hours after she was born.
Tonsfeldt gently collected the newborn and examined her in another room. She weighed 3½ pounds, roughly half that of an average full-term infant. He found no signs of injury or trauma.

The medical examiner still felt that something was awry. To play for time, he asked if someone would make him a cup of coffee and headed to the kitchen. As Tonsfeldt waited, one of the baby’s grandfathers approached him and blurted out an unexpected question: Would it make a difference if Ginnifer had a twin?
There was another baby, a girl named Evelyn. She was alive.
In the dim light of a bathroom, Tonsfeldt found women huddled over a tiny newborn, who was barely making a sound. They were feeding her from an eyedropper.

He told the family to get her to a hospital. After Evelyn’s grandfather made it clear they weren’t going anywhere, Tonsfeldt summoned the police, who delivered an ultimatum: Take Evelyn to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.

Evelyn’s family relented. A patrol car followed to make sure they got there. She was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit in Portland with respiratory distress syndrome. With the help of a breathing machine and a feeding tube, Evelyn began to stabilize. An autopsy would later conclude the same condition, common in premature babies, had caused her sister’s death.
The Mitchells were charged with murder by neglect, as well as criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical care. That left authorities with another challenge: Who would care for Evelyn?

Her family assumed any custody arrangement would be temporary and suggested Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, a couple born and raised in the Followers. But Marshall was no ordinary Follower. Once, when his young son became gravely ill, he brought him to a hospital. In the eyes of the state, that made Marshall and his wife suitable candidates to look after Evelyn.

Evelyn’s family didn’t know then that Marshall’s choice to save his son had set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. And that he would take Evelyn with him.

For more than a century, states have wrestled with how to address the deaths of children whose parents refuse them medical care for religious reasons. As early as 1901, a father in New York who believed in the “power of God to heal the sick through prayer” was prosecuted for failing to call a doctor for his young daughter who died from pneumonia. Since then, courts have repeatedly held — in cases where Christian Scientists refused treatment or Jehovah’s Witnesses declined blood transfusions — that adults are free to reject medical care for themselves.
Whether they can be compelled to provide medical care for their children is another matter, one that’s been left to states to decide. Courts have generally deferred to legislatures on this question.
Video: This Secretive Religious Sect Doesn’t Believe in Medical Care

Marshall Phillips was raised in the Followers of Christ, which forbids medical care. When his son fell gravely ill, he took him to the hospital. That choice set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known.

For decades, Oregon’s law gave latitude to faith healing and authorities did little to intervene. Between 1989 and 1999, 18 children of the Oregon City-based Followers died. (The sect numbered between 1,500 and 2,000 at its peak.) Most or all of those deaths were preventable, according to the state medical examiner at the time, who estimated that the child death rate in the sect was 26 times that of the general population.

The revelation of those deaths, in The Oregonian and other news outlets, prompted state lawmakers to act. In 1999, they removed spiritual treatment as a defense for second-degree manslaughter and criminal mistreatment. In 2008, prosecutors filed their first case against Followers parents after a 15-month-old died from untreated bronchial pneumonia and a blood infection. A jury convicted the girl’s father of a single count of criminal mistreatment, a misdemeanor, and acquitted her mother.

Two more children in the sect died without medical attention during this period, prompting the Legislature in 2011 to do away with the spiritual defense for any crime. Among those supporting the change: the Christian Science church, which by then had softened its stance amid a steep decline in membership. In a letter to lawmakers that year, a church official wrote: “Spiritual care should never be practiced at the expense of a child’s life.”

Changes in Oregon law — and prosecutors’ willingness to pursue parents who watched their children die — spurred a slow but perceptible shift: Deaths of children in the Followers have become an anomaly. Ginnifer Mitchell’s death in 2017 came amid that yearslong decline. Since then, one child has died due to lack of medical care.

During this same time frame in Idaho, where the laws protect parents who rely only on faith healing, reporting by ProPublica found at least 11 babies and children of Followers died from treatable conditions.

Still, Ginnifer’s death shows how the most entrenched elements of faith-healing communities resist aggressive enforcement. Sarah Mitchell chose to give birth without doctors or nurses, even as her sister was in prison for failing to provide medical care for her premature newborn, who died in 2009. And Sarah’s lack of prenatal care was such that she realized she was carrying twins only when her labor continued after her first baby emerged.
Evelyn might not have survived if police didn’t have the law on their side, allowing them to intervene and demand that her parents take her to the hospital.

The stories of Evelyn and Marshall Phillips — still the subject of legal proceedings today — offer a rare view into the closed community and reveal both the power and the limits of the state’s efforts to compel parents to seek medical care for their children.

Marshall’s ancestors were among the earliest members of the Followers, whose history dates to the late 1800s, when faith-healing sects were active in the Midwest. The faithful later migrated west, starting congregations in Idaho. In the 1930s, a charismatic Followers preacher named Walter White left Idaho for Oregon City, then a lively hub for the timber and paper industries. White’s emotional sermons earned him the moniker “the crying preacher.”

Followers believed the devout earned their place in the afterlife through good acts. They also believed that God heals. The doctrine stems from a passage in the Book of James, which proclaims “And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.” Seeking medical care was viewed as an abandonment of faith. Those who visited doctors risked being shunned.
By the 1950s, White broke ties with other Followers congregations. He later said that Christ had visited him in a dream and told him the world would soon end and so would baptisms.

White died in 1969 at age 67. Baptisms ended after that, effectively sealing the faithful from the outside world. The Followers never identified White’s successor. To this day, the congregation has no pastor. The lack of a spiritual leader seems only to have intensified members’ influence on one another.
The sect’s practices include other unusual elements: The Bible doesn’t figure in their services, which consist mostly of congregants singing hymns.

In many respects, Followers lead conventional lives. As a boy born in 1975, Marshall rode his bike, ate sugary treats, watched TV and listened to 1980s rock bands like Van Halen. His parents took him and his siblings camping and saved up for trips to Disneyland.

But his life was also circumscribed by his faith. Several times a week, he accompanied his parents to functions at the beige meetinghouse set back from busy Molalla Avenue in Oregon City. Starting at age 7, Followers’ children are separated by gender and age into their own pews. Marshall understood that he would grow up, and grow old, with the kids seated around him. He was instructed not to befriend kids outside the church. Followers considered them “worldly,” the sect’s derisive term for those focused on terrestrial, rather than celestial, concerns.

Like his peers, Marshall never visited a pediatrician. He was never vaccinated. His mom anointed his forehead with extra virgin olive oil when his head throbbed. He endured chicken pox and whooping cough and eventually recovered from both — proof, he believed, of God’s healing powers.
His parents, like others in the sect, made exceptions for dental care. They accepted the use of Novocain but refused the ibuprofen the dentist recommended to address lingering pain after a procedure.

Marshall knew from a young age that his future would be determined by the church. He figured he’d work for a Follower. He’d marry one, too. Marshall and Jennifer went on their first date in a courtship ritual the Followers call a carload — small groups of teens who drive together to get ice cream or coffee. She was 14 and he was 18. They married when Jennifer turned 17, the age girls in the Followers typically wed.

Jennifer’s father had died the year before, surrounded by men from the church. Members were expected to care for the dying, with men tending to men and women to women. Her father never went to the doctor, and family members think he died from heart failure. He was 37.

Women typically give birth in their parents’ homes, and Jennifer was no exception. She delivered her first child, Mary, in the living room, attended by her mother, her mother-in-law, aunts and other women. Marshall was there, too. The rest of the men waited out of sight, smoke from their cigarettes drifting into the living room. She had two more children after that, both sons.

Today, at 50, Marshall looks like the epitome of a suburban dad. With his receding hairline, beard and broad physique, you could picture him browsing the aisles of The Home Depot. He possesses a gentle quality and doesn’t shy away from even harsh self-reflection.

The Followers abide by what they view as traditional gender roles, with men leading their households. Many male Followers work as contractors, electricians and plumbers; Marshall works as a consultant for a heating and air conditioning company. Women mostly focus on the home and their children. Jennifer cleans houses to supplement their income and homeschooled their kids for a time.

As a Follower, Marshall said he pressured his children to fit in at church. He believed the sect’s teachings about earning one’s way to salvation, and he spent many Sunday afternoons visiting the sick and caring for the dying. He and his wife never challenged the institution that shaped their lives.

The couple saw no reason to visit the doctor or take their kids to one. That changed in the summer of 2013. They watched as their energetic preteen son, Nick, suddenly turned lethargic. Walking even a few feet left him out of breath, and he was soon confined to the couch.

His symptoms worsened over a matter of hours. As his extended family gathered to offer support, one relative wondered whether he had diabetes. Millions of Americans manage the condition with medication, but for a Follower, it could amount to a death sentence.

Marshall remembered that his cousin Bo had suffered from the disease more than a decade earlier. Bo Phillips developed flu-like symptoms and within days lapsed into a coma. He died in his parents’ bed at 11 — Nick’s age. A sheriff’s detective arrived to find Bo in a diaper, his body gaunt from dehydration. His fever was so high that his body registered a triple-digit temperature three hours after his death. He never went to a doctor.
As Marshall pondered what to do about Nick, he knew his relatives expected him to rely only on his faith in God. For a Follower, going to the hospital was unthinkable.

He knew that Followers had been prosecuted for failing to seek medical attention. He panicked at the thought that he — or worse, his wife — could go to prison if he chose not to take Nick to the hospital. Marshall felt trapped between his faith and the law.
He could see his son was struggling to breathe. The boy lay on the couch, barely conscious.
Marshall decided to act. “I’m taking him to the hospital,” he announced. In the same breath, he apologized.
Some family members expressed disapproval as he carried Nick to the door. One urged him not to turn away from God. Another whispered the name of a hospital where he should take the boy.

Marshall and Jennifer, who agreed with his decision, sped north on Interstate 5 to Legacy Emanuel Medical Center in North Portland. “Can you help my son?” he begged as he rushed into the emergency department, his unresponsive boy in his arms. Medical staff whisked him into the back, where a team quickly assessed Nick’s condition.

He had acute onset Type 1 diabetes. His blood was turning acidic, his organs shutting down. The Phillipses had arrived just in time. Without treatment, the doctors later said, he was hours from death.

That Marshall dwelled on his own fate as his son lay dying would leave him with a searing shame. “I wish I could be the great dad who jumped up and saw that his kid was sick and ran into the hospital,” he would say years later. “But I was weighing out the consequences. That’s the truth. And I’m not happy to say that.”

Marshall quickly grasped the implications of his decision. Relatives who had poured into the house to pray for Nick as he lay near death stopped coming around as he recovered. When the Phillipses tried to make holiday plans, some relatives didn’t reply. Nick’s closest friend stopped talking to him.

Marshall descended into depression. He turned to the Bible, scouring passages for proof that God forbade medical care. He found only references that showed how doctors were held in high esteem, such as Luke, whom Scripture refers to as a “beloved physician.”

On his commute to work, Marshall started listening to sermons of preachers from other denominations. He was moved by their messages of grace, forgiveness and redemption, concepts he’d never heard much about at church.

Over time, Marshall came to believe that God did heal — and he could use doctors to do it. He also came to believe that by saving his son, he had freed himself. And eventually that choice placed him at the center of another family’s tragedy.

When Evelyn arrived at the hospital a few hours after her birth in 2017, she was small even for a premature baby. She had been born about eight weeks early and weighed less than 4 pounds. Her glucose level was perilously low. She needed a feeding tube and a machine to help her breathe and remained in the neonatal intensive care unit for 11 days.

As criminal authorities investigated her parents, Evelyn’s fate rested with child welfare workers and a Clackamas County circuit judge. At a hearing to decide who would take care of Evelyn, lawyers for the Mitchells argued that Evelyn should come home with them while the investigation played out.

For child welfare officials and prosecutors, the proposal was out of the question. “These parents let this child’s twin die in their arms without making any effort at all to seek medical care,” one prosecutor told the judge. “And simultaneously they failed to seek medical care on behalf of this child and placed her also at extreme risk of death.” She continued: “We send parents to prison for failing to adequately undertake their duty to their children.”

On the stand, Marshall testified about his decision to take Nick to the hospital. He told the judge that his son was thriving and pledged to make sure Evelyn received medical care. (Evelyn’s grandfather had called him the night before to ask whether he’d be willing to take her in.)
Evelyn would stay with the Phillipses for now, the state decided.
Two days later, the couple drove to the hospital to meet Evelyn. She was so tiny that Jennifer’s mother bought her outfits from the doll aisle of Fred Meyer.

A year later, in the summer of 2018, Sarah and Travis Mitchell pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide for Ginnifer’s death and criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical help. The agreement called for the couple to spend six years and six months in prison — the harshest sentence ever handed down to parents in the sect.

The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to requests to be interviewed for this article.)

As part of their plea bargain, prosecutors insisted the Mitchells sign a statement. “We should have sought adequate medical care for our children,” it read, “and everyone in the church should always seek adequate medical care for our children.”
The district attorney instructed the Followers to post the message at their Oregon City meetinghouse.
The message was torn down later that day.

The Phillipses had begun attending services at an evangelical Christian church. The couple worried Followers would find out they were drifting away, so they picked a large out-of-the-way congregation where they figured it would be easy to go unnoticed. The church, like other mainstream evangelical congregations, encouraged its members to visit doctors.
Even then, Marshall didn’t sever the family’s ties with the Followers. He couldn’t face the prospect of walking away from his parents and people he’d known his entire life.

The Phillipses weren’t the only Followers questioning their faith. Around the same time, a loose network of men had been quietly meeting to pray and discuss the Bible. Starting in 2018, an estimated 150 to 200 people left the sect, an exodus spurred mostly by a desire to engage with the Bible. Many who walked away had also become disillusioned with the Followers’ rejection of medicine.
Like generations born into the sect after White’s death, Marshall had never been baptized. Doing so would offend the Followers.
But in the fall of 2018, he decided he could no longer ignore his desire to experience the rite. He saw it as a public expression of the spiritual shift he’d undergone. Jennifer did too.

One Sunday afternoon that October, the couple joined dozens of others on the muddy banks of the Willamette River. They waded into the water as a friend held a sleeping Evelyn, then 19 months old. By this point the state had made the Phillipses’ guardianship permanent.
The baptism spelled the end of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips’ time in the Followers. Before the ceremony, Marshall had texted his family to let them know it was happening.
Soon after, his mother texted him to say goodbye.
Earlier this year, Evelyn climbed into the back seat of the Phillipses’ car, a bouquet of tangerine-colored roses that she picked out resting on her lap.
It was March 5, her ninth birthday. Every year on this day, the couple drives Evelyn to the Followers cemetery to visit her twin sister’s grave.

Evelyn admired the stuffed bear she had charmed Marshall into buying. She especially liked the polka dot ribbon twirled around its neck. “I think if Ginny was here,” she said, “she would have liked this for her birthday.”

Marshall pulled up to the cemetery gate. The sect owns this land at the end of a rural two-lane road about 10 miles from downtown Oregon City. Generations of Followers are buried here. Among them: Evelyn’s great-great grandfather, Walter White, the sect’s founding pastor.
Ginnifer’s grave lies near a stand of evergreens. Evelyn knelt down. “I miss you, Ginny,” she said, placing the stuffed bear on the tombstone.

Nearby lay the grave of Hayden Edwards. He died two days after his birth in 2023. His parents were convicted of criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for him, the most recent faith-healing prosecution in Oregon.

Marshall walked the neat rows, passing a fresh grave, one that showed the limitations of Oregon’s laws. The state had stepped in several years ago when parents had refused to get medical treatment for their teenage son, who was experiencing renal failure. After prosecutors intervened, the parents agreed to a plea deal and made sure he got care. But when the son turned 18 this year, he declined further treatment. He died within days.

Marshall paused when he came to his own father’s headstone. It had “Dad” etched into the granite. He learned of his father’s death last year from a friend who heard the news from someone else. One of Marshall’s relatives called to let him know he wasn’t welcome at the funeral.

The day after the visit to the cemetery, guests filled the Phillipses’ home for Evelyn’s birthday party. Three-tiered display stands held homemade carrot cupcakes topped with swirls of cream cheese frosting — treats Evelyn had requested. Evelyn, ebullient, pinballed (and later roller-skated, using one birthday gift) between friends, parents and grandparents. Her long hair spilled out from under a pink helmet. The family had invited Evelyn’s birth parents, who joined them in the living room to watch her open gifts piled high on a table.

Evelyn first got to know them while they were in prison, and she knows why they were there. The couple spends time with her twice a month, taking her on adventures to the Oregon Zoo, roller skating and the park. She is their only child.
At the party, the Mitchells kept their focus on Evelyn, smiling broadly as she tore the wrapping from packages. They pulled out their phones to record her delight.
“Daddy!” Evelyn exclaimed at one point, marveling over one of her gifts.
Marshall and Travis both swiveled toward her in response.

The Phillipses’ friends filtered back into the kitchen. The Mitchells stayed behind. Their birthday card lay at one end of a table in the living room. “Not a day goes by where you aren’t missed, loved and thought of,” it read. “We thank God every day that we get to be a part of your life.” They signed it: “All our love, Dad & Mom.”
Travis ducked into the other room to look for Marshall. He thanked him for the evening. His wife had already slipped out of the house.
These days, brief exchanges with Travis are as close as Marshall comes to interacting with other Followers.

The Phillipses still live in Oregon City, home to most members of the sect. Marshall sees them, including his extended family, around town. Some ignore him. Others offer an obligatory nod. Rarely do they stop to talk. The Followers continue to gather every Thursday evening and Sunday morning without him.
Still, there are hints of change, albeit invisible ones. One former Follower told detectives in 2023 that some younger parents are quietly taking their children to the doctor.
For now at least, Evelyn is an outsider to the Followers. Marshall raised her that way. In June, she took a step that could further alienate her from the sect: She was baptized.

Four months after that, in October, tensions flared between Evelyn’s two sets of parents. The Mitchells filed a motion in court effectively seeking to terminate Marshall and Jennifer’s permanent guardianship — they acknowledged that Evelyn opposed the move — then withdrew the filing in November. (The Mitchells also criticized the Phillipses for allowing Evelyn to participate in this article.) The Mitchells are now seeking expanded visitation time with Evelyn.

Marshall wants Evelyn to determine her own future — to marry when she’s ready, not at 17. He talks to her about college, a possibility he wouldn’t have broached with his children as a Follower. Today he regrets how rigid he was, during his years in the sect, with his older children. Evelyn has brought out a paternal tenderness in him.
Some months ago, Jennifer took Evelyn to the pediatrician for a checkup. Evelyn swapped her school uniform for an oversized hospital gown that brushed the floor when she stood.
A cheery medical assistant stepped into the room. “She’s up to date with vaccines,” the woman announced. “We do offer the HPV at age 9. Do you want to do that today?”

Jennifer and Marshall weren’t vaccinated as kids, nor were their other children. Jennifer, who visited a doctor for the first time in her mid-40s, hadn’t heard about the HPV vaccine, which can prevent most cancers caused by the human papillomavirus. But she trusted Evelyn’s pediatrician. If vaccines were recommended, she wanted Evelyn to have them.
A physician assistant looked in Evelyn’s ears and shone a light in her eyes. She tapped her knees to check her reflexes. All signs pointed to a healthy girl.

“Now,” she said, “I’m going to listen to your lungs.” She placed a stethoscope on the girl’s chest, the sound of the ventilation system humming in the quiet room. Evelyn, whose lungs once nearly failed her, took a deep breath.
How We Reported This Story

Reporter Noelle Crombie relied on records from the Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office and the Clackamas County Sheriff’s Office, including detectives’ interviews with Sarah and Travis Mitchell, their parents and other members of the Followers of Christ; photographs taken during the execution of search warrants; investigative summaries by detectives and records obtained by investigators; Oregon City Police Department reports; recordings of the March 16, 2017, circuit court hearing where Evelyn’s initial custody status was determined and the July 9, 2018, hearing in Clackamas County Circuit Court where the Mitchells were sentenced; Clackamas County Circuit Court records; Clackamas County Department of Communications 911 audio recordings; Oregon City Police Department body-worn camera footage; Evelyn’s medical records from the OHSU Doernbecher Children’s Hospital, which her legal guardian Marshall Phillips obtained at The Oregonian/OregonLive’s request; historical legislative records in the Oregon State Archives; and archival records from the Followers of Christ. Crombie observed many of the interactions she describes in the story. For others, she relied on official records and the memories of those who were directly involved.
The post A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin. appeared first on ProPublica.

articles.title: Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher
articles.author: Noelle Crombie
paras: It was a stark and forbidding vision for those who followed the righteous path. Scorn, the preacher told his congregation, was a person’s lot if they led an “honest, clean, pure, godly life.” The world hated “people that live like that,” he said.
“They want you to be just as ungodly and filthy as they are,” he said in a rare audio recording, obtained by The Oregonian/OregonLive, of a 1958 sermon.

The preacher was Walter White, who led an Oregon City offshoot of the Followers of Christ, an Idaho sect that spurns medical treatment as a show of faith. White was a grocer, originally from Picabo, Idaho, whose congregants came to view as a prophet. He rambled at times during his sermon but always returned to simple and severe messages about choosing righteousness rather than the ways of the world. A trim figure in wire-rim glasses and dark combed-back hair, he spoke in a voice that evoked the stentorian tones of an old newsreel announcer. In the scratchy recording, people cough and babies cry as he preaches.

White was uneasy about being taped, according to a note by the congregant who made the recording. White didn’t want his message to fall into what he thought were undesirable hands. He viewed disbelievers with disgust. They put their trust in human experts, such as doctors, rather than in God. People like that, he told the faithful, “want to be somebody.” They want “the wisdom of the world and admiration.”

Today, nearly 60 years after White’s death, his pronouncements continue to influence the faithful. For many Followers, White remained “the highest authority,” said Mark Shaw, who left the sect in 2019 and keeps in touch with some Followers. Members invoked his teachings to settle disagreements. “It was used as the trump card,” he said. “It was the discussion-ender.”
To understand the modern-day Oregon City congregation, it’s essential to examine White’s role. No pastor ever succeeded him, leaving the sect all the more reliant on his teachings.

The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica have published a series of articles in recent months about the Followers of Christ in Oregon and Idaho, focusing on the long history of parents in Followers congregations declining to seek medical care for their critically ill children and the sometimes fatal consequences.

Little has been publicly known about White, likely due to the Followers’ culture of isolation and secrecy. The Oregonian/OregonLive was able to piece together details through documents we obtained, including biographical sketches, a transcript and the recording of the sermon, along with written accounts of dreams White purported to have and records of baptisms he performed. Among the documents was a list of his prophecies and even a sex guide he disseminated.

White was born into the Followers, whose members migrated to Idaho from the Midwest around the turn of the 20th century. Men in White’s family preached, and he joined them in his 20s, the story goes, after he dreamed that worms would devour him if he didn’t.

In the early 1930s, White joined two church elders on a journey from Idaho to Oregon City to minister to a dying man. After talking with them, the man readily discarded his medications and was relieved to see White, an avid smoker, roll a cigarette because the man didn’t want to kick the habit.
